title: Build the Minimum-Cost Power Grid
real_world_story: The utility has a list of all possible transmission lines it could build, each with a construction cost. It must choose a subset of these lines that connects every facility while spending as little as possible overall.

real_world_connection.input_represents: All candidate transmission lines and their construction costs
real_world_connection.output_represents: The minimum total cost to connect every facility
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Building a minimum spanning network (spanning tree)

problem_statement: Given N facilities numbered 0 to N-1 and E candidate undirected transmission lines with costs, find the minimum total cost required to connect all N facilities into a single connected grid.
task: Return the total cost of the minimum-cost spanning grid. If the graph cannot connect all facilities, return -1.
input_format: The first line contains two integers N and E. The next E lines each contain three integers u v w describing a candidate transmission line between facilities u and v with construction cost w.
output_format: Print the minimum total construction cost that connects all facilities, or -1 if they cannot all be connected.

examples.explanation: The cheapest way to connect all facilities uses the lines 2-3 (4), 0-3 (5) and 0-1 (10), for a total of 19.

expected_algorithm.name: Kruskal's Algorithm
expected_algorithm.reason: Sorting candidate lines by cost and adding the cheapest line that does not create a cycle yields the minimum-cost spanning tree.

hint: Sort all candidate transmission lines by construction cost.
Add each candidate in order if it connects two still-unconnected groups.
Use a union-find structure to track which facilities are already connected.
Stop once N - 1 lines have been selected.
real_world_takeaway: Kruskal's algorithm lets a utility build a fully connected grid at the minimum construction cost by choosing the cheapest non-redundant connections.
